view: Ghasaq describes darkness mixed with the first light at night's end or the lingering light after sunset.
Oaths should be read as evidence for the sura's claim and tested against parallel Quranic passages, rather than assumed to exalt sacred objects.
note: Bint al-Shati objects to turning every oath object into an honor symbol.

view: Explanations of the oath objects vary with whether their definite or indefinite forms and articles are read generally or specifically.
note: Ibn Ashur favors generic dawn because it is paired with night; Elmalili favors a particular feast dawn for its shared joy.

view: Al-Tabari cautions against claims unsupported by reports or reason, while al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari criticize expansive speculation about the oaths.
Quranic oath formulas may draw on a characteristic expression of pre-Islamic soothsayers, though this historical link is insufficiently studied.
The sura uses varied scenes, rhythms, and rhyme to unite devotional beauty with warning, history, and moral correction.
Ibn Abbas reads 'nights of ten' with an annexation, making the nights those of ten days.
After Muadh's prolonged prayer drove a man away, the Prophet rebuked him and recommended short suras for prayer, including al-Fajr.
note: The other examples begin with glorification, the sun, and night.

view: A Prophetic report interprets the ten as the ten days of sacrifice, the odd as Arafah, and the even as the Day of Sacrifice.
A report calls dawn the familiar dawn, the ten nights the ten of sacrifice, the even creation in pairs, and the odd God.
The Prophet calls Muharram God's month and the best time for voluntary fasting after Ramadan, and night prayer the best prayer after obligatory prayer.
Ali recommended fasting Muharram after Ramadan, saying it includes a day when God accepted one people's repentance and forgave others.
Ibn Shihab fasted Ashura during travel because a missed Ramadan fast could be made up later, whereas Ashura would pass.
Reports promise abundant provision through the year to one who gives generously to family on Ashura.
note: Al-Bayhaqi says the individually weak chains strengthen one another.

view: A report says antimony applied to the eyes on Ashura prevents eye inflammation forever; al-Bayhaqi judged it weak.
Surat al-Fajr is Meccan, often described as early Meccan; an alternative calls it Medinan.
note: Ibn al-Zubayr and Ibn Abbas transmit the Meccan classification; Tabatabai grounds it in the sura's context.

view: The sura has thirty verses according to one count; another gives twenty-nine, and regional counts differ.
The sura followed al-Layl in revelation; one account calls it tenth in revelation order and places al-Duha after it.
A report promises forgiveness to one who recites al-Fajr and light on Resurrection Day to one who recites it daily.
The sura condemns worldly attachment, tyranny, ingratitude, and the mistaken belief that wealth proves divine favor or poverty humiliation; both conditions test preparation for the afterlife.
note: Judgment will expose the choice of punishment over reward.

view: The tranquil soul submits to God, remains steady through gain and loss, and receives the promised peaceful outcome.
The basmala depicts God gathering scattered people, granting clarifying guidance and faith, and reserving contentment and gardens for His chosen servants.
A cultic understanding of the ten nights remains persuasive despite objections to Neuwirth's liturgical reading of cosmic oath sequences.
The harmony of opposed natural forces points to one wise and powerful sovereign; rival deities would destroy that harmony.
Without a Day of Judgment, good and evil would be treated alike and creation would lack purpose.
Night and daylight sustain material life; ease and hardship train gratitude and patience, preparing the person for the tranquil state described later.
Night and day alternate under God's control; the signs of release and restraint show that even powerful people cannot escape Him, and perpetual night or day would be possible by His will.

Reports about Dhu al-Hijjah's nights, Arafah, and the Sacrifice Day best fit the oath sequence and sura's purpose, gathering its possible senses and urging worship within life's limited time for afterlife joy.
The Prophet warns through signs in heaven and earth even when people fail to see them; he cannot make the blind accept guidance.
Al-fajr denotes dawn alongside even and odd, the withdrawing night, and intellect in the subsequent oaths.
Fasting Ashura is urged, with the ninth or an adjacent day to distinguish Muslim practice from Jewish practice; a report says Jews treated it as a festival and prophets had fasted it.
Al-Ghashiyah's ending announces return and reckoning; this sura renews that warning through God's watchfulness, while the dawn and pilgrims' rites evoke rising again to reward or punishment.
note: Al-Biqai specifies sleepers rising from death-like sleep, pilgrim clothing, talbiya, and travel; Islahi reasons that wisdom and mercy require accountability.

view: The sura follows al-Ghashiyah's two kinds of faces with arrogant deniers and the blessed tranquil soul; its opening oaths reinforce the prior promise and threat and echo its opening questions.
Dawn's opposition to departing night ties the first and last oaths together; the ten nights and middle oaths stand between and elaborate the night side.
note: The ten nights uniquely quantify night among parallel Quranic dawn and night oaths.

view: The succession of dawn, crescent, and night turns physical light emerging from darkness into an image of truth after tyranny and prepares the sura's tests and opposed outcomes.
The oaths' cosmic contrasts of dawn/night and even/odd resemble other Quranic oath sequences, where natural duality anticipates good and evil and their different afterlife recompense.
note: Islahi adds that this world's incomplete moral pairs call for an afterlife to complete judgment.

view: The opening oath resembles oath openings in earlier suras 93, 95, 100, and 103 and roughly contemporary suras 91 and 92.
note: The commentary refers readers to its discussion of the oath type at 93:1–2.

view: The basmala unsettles the poor and disorients the enamored but grants lovers mercy; worshippers satisfy it by recitation, whereas lovers offer their lives.
Fajr is the first light or time of daybreak: darkness splits at the horizon and daylight begins to appear.
note: The word is also used by extension for the time of the light's appearance.

view: The root evokes splitting or bursting forth, as with water emerging from earth; related words describe a person breaking from obedience.
note: Bint al-Shati prefers the broader idea of emergence or outburst over deriving all uses narrowly from splitting.

view: Arabic applies the root to emergence in light, goodness, generosity, and virtue, and to emergence in evil, sin, or transgression; the Fijar days were four pre-Islamic battle days.

The root occurs twenty-four times in the Quran; its verbs mostly concern water gushing, its noun can name rivers or a spring, and it also denotes wickedness opposite piety. Dawn occurs in six verses, whose imagery locates its white light after night darkness.
note: One non-water verbal use refers to transgression; 2:187 uses the white thread as a dawn sign.

view: Unlike fajr, which marks the moment darkness gives way at the horizon, subh extends from dawn through the time after sunrise and is therefore qualified in other oaths.
Kufan grammarians describe dawn's light as white; Medinan grammarians call it red, citing Arabic use of the word for a red-dyed garment.
note: The disagreement concerns the color associated with dawn's light.

view: Dawn has a narrow upright first streak, sometimes called false dawn because it can mislead, followed by true dawn, whose light spreads horizontally.
note: The false dawn is likened to a wolf's tail; al-Tabrisi calls its upright light an announcement that night is ending.

view: A cited poem calls true dawn al-musaddiq, the truthful one, because it reliably signals morning.
The oath's waw governs al-fajr in the genitive.
An omitted noun may be supplied before fajr, yielding an oath by the Lord of dawn, the dawn prayer, or the Quran recited at dawn.
Grammarians dispute the name of the rhyme-like nunation: some prefer tanwin tark al-tarannum to tanwin al-tarannum; tanwin al-ghali belongs to closed rhyme and has different, disputed rules.
God swears by dawn as one of five opening oaths.
The oath's stated answer is 'Your Lord is surely watching' in 89:14: God knows and recompenses deeds.
note: Al-Razi treats the intervening passage as parenthetical.

view: The oath's answer is implicit: God will requite each person, seize or punish oppressors, vindicate the wronged, and bring resurrection, judgment, punishment, and reward; the stories of earlier peoples indicate it.
note: Al-Zamakhshari supplies 'He will surely punish,' citing the earlier peoples' destruction.

view: The oath's omitted answer is inferred from al-Ghashiyah's ending: people return to God for reckoning.
note: Abu Hayyan and Muhammad Abdu ground this in the preceding sura's placement.

view: An answer supplied by al-Ghashiyah is rejected because al-Ghashiyah was revealed fifty-eight suras after al-Fajr, so adjacency in the printed Quran cannot supply this oath's response.
note: This disputes the preceding-sura answer.

view: The oath's answer is implicit in what was brought to Abraham and Muhammad.
The surrounding passage should be read as an appeal to admonition and reflection.
Abu al-Dinar al-Arabi nunates al-fajr and other oath endings, treating their pauses like poetic rhyme endings; most readers omit this nunation.
note: Ibn Khalawayh calls this tanwin al-tarannum and compares Arabic pauses even on verbs or definite nouns; poems and Quranic parallels are cited.

view: The oath concerns the familiar dawn or morning light that breaks each day, with no restriction to a particular date.
note: Some notes call it generic dawn, others specify every day's dawn; these agree against the proposed named dates.

view: Al-fajr means the entire daytime, named for its beginning at dawn.
note: Bint al-Shati rejects this in favor of dawn at night's end; Tabatabai calls it a poor proposal.

view: Al-fajr refers to the dawn prayer, in some accounts including its recitation or the Quran of dawn.
note: Al-Razi adds that night and day angels gather to hear its recitation; Tabatabai calls the proposal poor.

view: The dawn is the first dawn of Muharram, the year's beginning.
note: Some pair this dawn with Muharram's first ten nights; al-Razi mentions yearly rites and a report praising Muharram, while Tabatabai calls this identification poor.

view: The dawn is the first dawn of Dhu al-Hijjah, linked to the following ten nights and the opening of pilgrimage rites.
note: Some notes say only 'dawn of Dhu al-Hijjah'; the stated reason is its pairing with the ten nights.

view: The dawn is the morning of the Day of Sacrifice, the tenth of Dhu al-Hijjah, when the ten nights end and sacrifice and pilgrimage rites take place.
note: Al-Qurtubi gives the preceding-night and pilgrimage-deadline argument; al-Biqai mentions entering the sanctuary, leaving consecration, and God's hospitality; Bursevi specifies circumambulation, shaving, and stoning. Elmalili prefers its collective joy. Tabatabai calls the identification poor.

view: The dawn is Friday's dawn.
note: Elmalili presents Friday as a blessed special dawn; Tabatabai calls the identification poor.

view: The dawn is the dawn of the night at Jamʿ or Muzdalifah during pilgrimage.
note: Ibn Ashur connects it with the Sacrifice Day dawn at Muzdalifah; Tabatabai calls the identification poor.

view: The dawn is the last of the ten days, when pilgrims depart from Jamʿ.
The dawn is the morning of Arafah, when pilgrims go to the plain and supplicate; a report says, 'Hajj is Arafah.'
The dawn is the start of each new year, without a specified month.
note: Other notes specify Muharram separately.

view: The dawn is Ramadan's dawn, paired with its last ten nights when the Quran was first revealed.
Fajr refers to springs or water bursting from rock and elsewhere, whose flow sustains life.
note: Tabatabai calls this proposal poor.

view: The imagery of things breaking forth includes miraculous water from the Prophet's fingers or Moses' stone, Salih's she-camel from rock, rain, and sinners' tears.
A Prophetic report identifies the dawn and ten nights with the ten days of sacrifice; one later account says al-Tabari accepted it because the interpreters agreed.
The opening oaths draw attention to valuable signs and blessings that point to the Creator and divine lordship.
note: Elmalili stresses worldly change from darkness to light and grief to joy; Islahi stresses God's sole control of bringing forth, removing, and granting respite.

view: Dawn's light, awakening life, and creatures setting out for provision offer an image of resurrection: as morning follows night and waking follows sleep, people will rise for judgment.
note: Islahi mentions a waking supplication; al-Razi also notes both true and false dawn.

view: The appearance of dawn after receding night serves as evidence that Judgment is an appointed, momentous event, as in al-Muddaththir.
Dawn is a gentle, joyful return of life in a waking world; creation seems to pray as it opens.
Dawn's image urges stained sinners to wash themselves with tears of repentance.
A likely authentic poem by Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt greets the Lord at every dawn, supporting a cultic or liturgical association for dawn.
The upright false dawn remains legally night and does not set prayer or fasting times; the spreading true dawn does.
note: Alusi considers true dawn especially apt for the oath because of these rules.

view: God may swear by any created thing, while people may swear only by God.
Dawn is Muhammad: through him the lights of faith and obedience, and the lights of both worlds, emerge and unbelief's darkness disappears.
Dawn is the opening worship of the saints.
Dawn is the time when beloveds commune with God.

In a reading of the great resurrection, dawn is divine light appearing in the soul's night; the following oaths describe dormant senses, witness and witnessed, oneness after duality, and selfhood disappearing.

In a reading of death as the lesser resurrection, dawn is the sun rising from the west; the following oaths portray dimmed senses, spirit and body, the spirit's separation, and bodily darkness dispersing.
